summary:
We developed "CosmIO", a citizen-science game that turns NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey into an interactive astronomical investigation experience. Players explore real observations, investigate moving and variable sources, examine infrared spectra, compare observations across time, and contribute classifications and findings. 

Underpinning the game is our SPHEREx Explorer scientific engine, which retrieves and processes SPHEREx observations, performs image and spectral analysis, cross-references astronomical catalogues, and provides a 3D atlas of hundreds of thousands of real astronomical objects. These capabilities power investigations that encourage players to think and work like astronomers.

Through investigation challenges, experience points, achievements, daily streaks, player profiles and competitive leaderboards, we make participation engaging while rewarding meaningful contributions. Automated quality checks and community review help assess submissions without confusing preliminary findings with scientifically confirmed discoveries.

Our project addresses the challenge of making large astronomical datasets accessible and meaningful. By combining real scientific infrastructure with citizen-science gameplay, we aim to turn public curiosity into active participation in exploring the infrared universe.
details:
CosmIO — A Citizen-Science Game for Exploring the Universe

What does it do and how does it work?

CosmIO is a citizen-science game built around a scientific platform that allows users to investigate NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey. Rather than simply viewing astronomical images, players take on the role of cosmic detectives, exploring real observations, investigating astronomical sources and contributing findings.

The game uses the scientific capabilities of our SPHEREx Explorer engine to power its investigations, complemented by an interactive SPHEREx Atlas that allows users to explore the wider astronomical environment.

Scientific investigations

Players can undertake several types of scientific investigations:

  • Moving-object investigations: Compare SPHEREx observations across different epochs, examine source positions and investigate objects displaying potential movement.
  • Variable-source investigations: Examine changes in brightness over time using light curves and identify potentially variable astronomical sources.
  • Spectral investigations: Explore the infrared spectral information of astronomical objects and investigate their characteristics.
  • Source classification: Examine astronomical objects and contribute classifications using available observational and catalogue information.
  • Candidate verification: Investigate unusual sources, compare evidence and participate in reviewing other players' findings.

The scientific engine retrieves SPHEREx observations from NASA/IPAC IRSA, aligns images onto a common sky grid, and provides time-lapse visualisation, image comparisons, metadata and analysis tools. It measures source motion, brightness variations and spectral information, and cross-references findings against catalogues including Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020. Potentially unusual objects are identified as candidates rather than automatically declared discoveries.

The SPHEREx Atlas

Beyond individual investigations, CosmIO features an interactive SPHEREx Atlas, a 3D visualisation of the stellar neighbourhood containing 573,000 objects, alongside additional SIMBAD sources and planetary systems from the NASA Exoplanet Archive.

Users can explore the sky by entering any Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) coordinates, allowing them to navigate to virtually any point in the celestial sphere rather than being restricted to predefined astronomical objects. The Atlas provides a way to investigate specific regions of the sky, discover nearby astronomical sources and explore their associated information through interactive visualisations.

The Atlas brings together astronomical positions, distances, object classifications and planetary system data to connect individual observations to the wider structure of our stellar neighbourhood. Planetary systems can also be explored through orbital visualisations and an optional N-body simulation engine, with Solar System simulations checked against NASA JPL Horizons.

How does the game encourage participation?

We combine scientific investigation with game mechanics to encourage sustained participation and reward meaningful contributions.

The platform includes:

  • Player profiles, experience points and progression levels.
  • Daily investigation challenges and login streaks.
  • Achievements and badges recognising different investigative milestones.
  • A Global Contribution Leaderboard, rewarding useful contributions following automated quality checks.
  • A separate Scientifically Validated Leaderboard, reserved for contributions that receive authoritative scientific recognition.
  • A collective community progress system that reflects participation in investigations.

Automated checks and community agreement help assess the quality of contributions, but are not presented as authoritative scientific validation. The platform is designed to operate independently, while providing a foundation for potential future collaboration with scientific researchers and institutions.

What are the benefits and intended impact?

Accessibility: Complex astronomical datasets become explorable through an interactive experience that does not require specialist software or prior astronomical knowledge.

Scientific education: Players learn through direct engagement with real observations, developing an understanding of infrared astronomy, spectral analysis, celestial coordinates, source detection and astronomical motion.

Citizen science: The game creates opportunities for people to contribute classifications, investigate unusual sources and participate in collaborative analysis.

Exploration and discovery: The SPHEREx Atlas allows users to navigate the celestial sphere using their own coordinates, discover astronomical objects and explore the relationships between stars and planetary systems.

Sustained engagement: Challenges, progression and competitive leaderboards provide incentives for players to return and continue investigating.

Scientific transparency: Observations and results retain their provenance. The platform distinguishes between measured, derived, predicted and display-only information, communicates uncertainty, and avoids presenting unmatched objects as discoveries.

Our intended impact is to bridge the gap between professional astronomy and public participation. We want to transform the exploration of SPHEREx data from a passive viewing experience into an active, collaborative investigation of the universe.

Tools and technologies

Backend and scientific computing

  • Python 3.11
  • FastAPI
  • NumPy and SciPy
  • Astropy
  • photutils
  • reproject

Frontend and visualisation

  • React and TypeScript
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Vite
  • three.js for interactive 3D visualisation
  • Aladin Lite for astronomical sky imagery
  • Plotly for scientific charts and analysis

Astronomical data and services

  • NASA SPHEREx data through NASA/IPAC IRSA
  • Gaia DR3
  • SIMBAD
  • CatWISE2020
  • NASA Exoplanet Archive
  • NASA JPL Horizons

Deployment and testing

  • Docker
  • Automated backend and frontend testing
  • A one-command application startup workflow

The application requires no specialised hardware and can run on an ordinary laptop.

What makes the project creative?

Our central idea is to turn an astronomical survey into a scientific investigation game. Instead of simplifying astronomy into quizzes or simulated exercises, we allow players to engage with the same underlying observational data and analysis capabilities that power the scientific explorer.

The project combines two complementary approaches to astronomical exploration: the SPHEREx Explorer, where users investigate individual observations and potential scientific anomalies, and the SPHEREx Atlas, where users freely navigate the sky and explore the wider stellar neighbourhood through celestial coordinates and 3D visualisation.

Together, these features connect different scales of astronomical exploration, from individual infrared observations and moving sources to planetary orbits and the wider stellar environment, while giving players opportunities to investigate the changing infrared sky.

We also treat scientific honesty as part of the experience. The platform distinguishes measurements from predictions, displays uncertainty, preserves data provenance and avoids making unsupported discovery claims. This ensures that making astronomy engaging does not come at the expense of scientific credibility.

What factors did our team consider?

Our development considered several important factors:

  • Scientific accuracy: Units, wavelengths, astronomical data releases, source measurements and instrument characteristics were considered and independently reviewed.
  • Uncertainty and reliability: Measurement uncertainties are communicated, and potential discoveries remain candidates until appropriately validated.
  • Data provenance: Scientific classifications identify whether they originate from SPHEREx measurements, existing catalogues or machine-learning predictions.
  • Accessibility: The platform uses publicly available astronomical data and requires no specialised hardware for viewers.
  • Performance: Caching and incremental data loading help manage large astronomical datasets.
  • Reproducibility: Documented data contracts, locked dependencies, shareable links and automated tests support reliable operation.
  • Collaboration: Our five-person team divided development across data acquisition, image processing, visualisation, scientific analysis, and API/application integration.

Ultimately, CosmIO combines a scientifically grounded astronomical platform with an engaging citizen-science experience, allowing the public to become active participants in exploring the infrared universe.
